job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Colin Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a desk by 8 in a small mortgage broker's office, where I'm a trainee credit analyst. I studied finance and economics and started in September. I check applicants' payslips and credit files, write up a summary for the adviser and use an AI tool for most of the first draft. I rent a room in a house of five lads, I go to mass on Sunday with my gran, and on Saturdays I sell vintage trainers online, which is my little business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful and a bit overrated. I'd tell my mates that it saves time on the dull bits and the job still needs a person who has some sense. Anyone who panics about it hasn't used it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in a good position for that world. I use the tools every day and I'm quicker than the senior analyst on a clean file. The worry isn't the tech, it's money. I owe about twenty-two thousand and my room takes half my pay. If the housing market stalls, a mortgage broker is the first to feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job well and grow the trainer business, which already brings about 200 a month. I'd put that straight onto my debt. I'd also ask my boss, Mr Brennan, if I can start taking on small clients myself once I'm qualified. Own-name work is where the money is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Driven. I like it when things don't shift under me and I can get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the trainer business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I buy pairs at car boot sales and from people's wardrobes, clean them up, photograph them and sell them online. I started in second year. The trainer business teaches you pricing, patience and how to talk to a stranger. It's the best thing I learned at university, and it wasn't on the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How safe do you think the mortgage broking job is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than most, because people still want someone to hold their hand through a big purchase. But if the market falls, the office would trim staff, and the newest one goes first. That's me. So I keep the trainers going as insurance.

say: It's useful and a bit **overrated**, and it saves time on the dull bits.
Anyone who panics about it **hasn't used it** much.
think: My worry isn't the tech, it's **money**: I owe about twenty-two thousand.
If the housing market stalls, a **mortgage broker** is the first to feel it.
do: Grow the **trainer business**, which brings in about 200 a month, and put it on the debt.
Ask Mr Brennan about taking my own **small clients** once qualified.
feel: **Good and driven**, liking it when things stay steady.
S0.quote: The trainer business teaches you pricing, patience and how to talk to a stranger.
fieldNote: Already has a **side business** and treats it as insurance.
Fully at ease with AI, and sees **panic** as a lack of use.
Mood is uneasy because the **housing market** and his debt are on his mind.

steps.text: Sell 15 more pairs of vintage trainers a month online
Put the whole 200 a month straight onto the debt
Use AI to draft file summaries faster and show Mr Brennan the results

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift, and the people who work hard and learn fast will do fine. I'd say governments shouldn't smother it with rules, and people shouldn't wait for handouts. I'd tell my mates to use the tools or get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think file checking and summaries are mostly done by the AI already. I just edit. If a broker with AI does the work of two analysts, the office trims to one. I'm good with the tools, but I'm also the newest and the cheapest, so I could go either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who runs the AI workflow in the office and show Mr Brennan the time we saved. I'd get qualified quickly so I can bring in my own clients. I'd double the trainer business and try a second line, like selling second-hand sports gear. And I'd save a six-week cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pumped, with an edge of nerves. I like being ahead of the pack, but I'm not going to pretend I'm immune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say governments shouldn't smother it. What would you want from them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Low taxes on small businesses and a fast way to get a licence or a qualification. Apprenticeships over classroom time. The rest is up to us. My gran ran a market stall for thirty years and never asked for a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle it if you were let go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go full time on the business and look for a short contract in a bigger firm. I'd move into a cheaper house too. I've been poor before, so I know I can eat beans for six months.

say: It's a big shift, and people who work hard and **learn fast** will do fine.
think: File checking and summaries are mostly done by the AI, and I **just edit**.
I'm good with the tools, but also the **newest and cheapest**.
do: Become the **AI workflow** person and show Mr Brennan the time saved.
Get **qualified** quickly and double the trainer business.
feel: **Pumped**, with an edge of nerves, and not pretending to be immune.
S1.quote: My gran ran a market stall for thirty years and never asked for a thing.
fieldNote: Wants **less state** and quicker qualifications, in line with his free-market view.
His gran's **market stall** is his model for self-reliance.
Mood is anxious because his **junior role** is exposed even with skill.

steps.text: Build the office's AI file-checking routine and show the time saved
Add a second online line selling second-hand sports gear
Sit the mortgage adviser qualification this year
Save a six-week cushion before spending on anything else

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll cope, because people always do, but I'd say the government can't be the answer. Two years is a shock, so families, churches and businesses have to step up. I'd tell my mates to get something that's their own, however small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the one that scares me. If AI does nearly all thinking work in two years, my edge, using it daily, goes. I'd be 24 with a pass degree and debt, and every broker could do my job at the touch of a button. The trainers are my lifeboat, but they're a small one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw everything at the business: I'd get the trainers up to a proper online shop, with a few other categories, and push the profit towards debt and a six-month cushion. I'd stay at the broker as long as they'd have me. I'd cut my costs to bare bones and move into the cheapest room I can find. I'd go to mass more, and lean on my gran and my uncle who runs a garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky. I've always thought I could work my way out of anything, and this is the first time I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've always thought you could work your way out of anything. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If machines do the work, there isn't a market for my hours. Hard work only pays when someone needs it. I'd have to hope enough people still want something that comes from a person, like a pair of trainers or a handshake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the shop would last past 2031 when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retail would be hit later, so I'd have a few years. I'd be selling to customers who need someone who knows what they're doing. I'd call it a bridge, not a plan. The plan is to keep adapting every year.

say: We'll cope, but the **government** can't be the answer, and two years is a shock.
Families, churches and businesses have to **step up**, and everyone should own something small.
think: If AI does nearly all thinking work, my **daily AI edge** goes.
The trainers are my **lifeboat**, but a small one.
do: Turn the trainers into a proper **online shop** and put profit on debt and a cushion.
Move to the **cheapest room**, and lean on my gran and my uncle's garage.
feel: **Shaky**, for the first time unsure I can work my way out.
S2.quote: Hard work only pays when someone needs it.
fieldNote: His **work-ethic** worldview is shaken, and he says so.
Turns to **family and church**, in line with his traditional outlook.
Expects his analyst role to go and has debt, so **alarmed**.

steps.text: Build the trainer business into a full online shop
Move into the cheapest room I can find
Build a six-month cushion before debt overpayments
Ask my uncle about weekend work at his garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run, and it will separate people who prepare from people who complain. I'd tell my mates to build something that's theirs. I'd also say that the best help is a chance to work, not a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. By 27 I could be a qualified adviser with a small book of clients, or running the business full-time. I'd have cleared the debt. The risk is that AI makes the broker's job a button and cuts out advisers altogether by 2031. I'd have to be a step ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify in year one and get my own clients, small ones to begin. I'd turn the trainer business into a registered company and hire a part-time helper. I'd then add a service like helping first-time buyers use AI tools to compare mortgages, which I know better than most. And I'd save a third of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up. It's the sort of timeline I like: short enough to focus me, long enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would first-time buyers pay for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're scared of mortgages. If I'm a face they trust, I explain it, show them the AI results and take a fee. They want a person to look in the eye. It's what my gran's market customers wanted: someone honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rules change, a platform does it for free and I'm squeezed out. So I'd have the trainers as a second leg. I never want one income. My dad lost a job at forty and we nearly lost the house. I won't be that exposed.

say: Five years separates people who **prepare** from people who complain.
The best help is a chance to **work**, not a cheque.
think: By 27 I could be a qualified adviser with a **small book of clients**.
The risk is AI making the broker's job a **button** by 2031.
do: Qualify in year one, win **small clients** and register the trainer business as a company.
Add a service helping **first-time buyers** use AI tools to compare mortgages.
feel: **Fired up**: short enough to focus me, long enough to build something.
S3.quote: My dad lost a job at forty and we nearly lost the house. I won't be that exposed.
fieldNote: His **father's job loss** at forty explains his drive for a second income.
Wants a **trusted face** business, a human angle on AI.
Mood stays anxious as **debt** and an exposed role remain.

steps.text: Qualify as a mortgage adviser and take on small clients
Register the trainer business as a company and hire a part-time helper
Spend 300 on a simple site and ads for first-time buyer advice
Save a third of every month's income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a big opening for people who want to build something. I'd tell friends to start now, save and don't count on anyone to save them. I'd also say that families should be ready to support each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, even excited. At 32 I could have my own firm, a house, a family and a few staff. My worry is that I'd be too comfortable and miss the moment, or build something just as the machines take it. But ten years gives me three or four tries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for two or three years, pay off the debt and qualify. Then I'd start my own brokerage or advice firm, partly with AI tools, with trust as its selling point. I'd hire a couple of young people and train them properly, as an apprenticeship. I'd marry, buy a house near my gran, and keep the trainers going just for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, and a bit impatient. I'd want to get started tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says this is just wishful thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say plans can be wrong, but not having one is worse. I've started small things and some have failed. A failed trainer batch costs 300, not a career. If you start small, you can afford to be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you look after your staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay them fairly, train them and be honest about the risks. If a tool replaced their job, I'd tell them early and help them find the next thing. I'd rather be a boss I'd want to work for.

say: Ten years is a **big opening** for people who want to build something.
Start now, save, and **don't count on anyone** to save you.
think: At 32 I could have my **own firm**, a house, a family and a few staff.
Ten years gives me **three or four tries**.
do: Pay off the debt, qualify, then start my own **advice firm** built on trust.
Hire two young people and run it as an **apprenticeship**.
feel: **Hopeful and impatient**, wanting to start tomorrow.
S4.quote: A failed trainer batch costs 300, not a career. If you start small, you can afford to be wrong.
fieldNote: Calm because **time** and a side business make his income feel secure.
Plans to treat staff **fairly** and warn them early about tools.
Small bets are his **philosophy**: start small so you can afford to be wrong.

steps.text: Clear the debt and qualify as an adviser within three years
Open my own small brokerage and advice firm by 2031
Train two apprentices properly and warn them early about new tools
Buy a house near my gran and marry

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole plan runs on hard work and a market for it. If both disappear, I'd have a business that depends on people having spare cash. What would help is ways for small businesses to keep going, cheap training that leads to real work and families and churches that stay close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not naive about this. I use the tools every day, and I'm still frightened. Being quick doesn't protect you. Being independent and having people around you does.

headlineQuote: Being quick doesn't protect you. Being independent and having people around you does.
portrait: Colin is a **22-year-old** trainee credit analyst at a mortgage broker, renting a room and owing about twenty-two thousand.
He uses AI every day and runs a **vintage trainer** business on the side, taught by his gran's market stall.
He is traditional and free-market: faith, family and self-reliance over state help.
He moves early in every scenario, with a **second income** as insurance, shaped by his father's job loss.
His mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, and to calm with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his daily AI edge and hard work might not find a market.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **small businesses**, cheap training that leads to real work, and family and church staying close.
